newsitem.title: USA: CME pork bellies rally at close, hogs end easier.
newsitem.headline: CME pork bellies rally at close, hogs end easier.

text.p: CME pork belly futures rallied sharply late from hefty early losses and ended over 2.000 cents higher in some months on demand linked to bullish storage and cash ideas, traders said. Hogs ended mostly lower.

Pork bellies fell early on long liquidation and pressure in back months from USDA's crop report, which could indicate increased pork output in the long term. But bellies rebounded on short covering and local and commission house demand.

Expectations for a bullish CME out-of-town report, stronger midday prices on 14-16 lb cash bellies and ideas of reduced kills in the near term sparked a late rally that took some months sharply higher, traders said.
Pork bellies closed 1.975 to 0.075 cent a lb higher with February up 1.875 at 74.100 cents.
Projections the storage report could show stocks less than a year ago provided much of the late strength.
"Very shortly we are going to end up with a lot less bellies in storage than a year ago," said Bill Cipolla, pork belly trader for Iowa Grain.
But after the futures close, the CME reported a net in-movement of 2.8 million lbs last week, above analysts' estimates of 1.5 to 2.0 million lbs.
Analysts are now looking for belly futures to show weaken early Wednesday.
"It (the CME data) is going to put downward pressure to start with (Wednesday)," said Chuck Levitt, senior livestock analyst for Alaron Trading Corp.

Hog futures ended 0.300 cent a lb higher to 0.950 lower with only December posting a gain at 58.225 cents. Deferreds posted losses following the USDA grain report which indicated greater-than-expected corn and soybean production and likely increased hog production next year.

The grain report was bullish to the nearby contracts because some gilts could be kept out of the slaughter mix and put back into the breeding herd. However, the grain data was seen bearish to deferred hog contracts because those retained gilts would ultimately mean increased hog and pork production.
However, trade in December was uneven as it holds a large premium to cash, traders said.
Talk that packers will be cutting slaughter rates weighed on sentiment at times while continued lighter than expected hog marketings lent support.
"It's not a very clear situation at this point," said Dale Durchholz, AgriVisor Services Inc market analyst. He noted that packers are cutting back kills by reducing Saturday kills.
It is hard to decide if they are cutting kills because they are not showing a profit or because hog supplies are tight, he said.
